optimization_strategy.strategy_name: Solar Duck Curve (OFF_PEAK solar hours - no discharge)
optimization_strategy.rationale: Tariff_window is OFF_PEAK and day_type is solar_duck_curve at 13:00 (within the solar valley period). The solar_duck_curve strategy specifies Phase 1 (10:00-15:00): shave_target = 0 kW (no discharge during cheapest solar hours) and charging is allowed when SOC < 80%. Current SOC is 90% (0.9), which is already above both the strategy’s SOC threshold for charging (<80%) and the general 10–95% safety envelope. Also, load forecast (~894–908 kW) is far above the given MD limit (800 kW), so discharging now to shave would consume SOC that is better reserved for the later duck-ramp/surge window; additionally, this tick cannot be charged above 95% SOC anyway. Therefore, optimal action this interval is 0 kW discharge (shave_kw=0) to preserve SOC reserve and follow the duck-curve timing risk control.

optimization_strategy.strategy_name: Solar Duck Curve (Phase 1 charging / no discharge mid-day)
optimization_strategy.rationale: Tariff window is OFF_PEAK and day_type is solar_duck_curve at 13:30 (within the Solar Valley window). The load forecast for the next interval is high (~901–916 kW), but OFF_PEAK energy is cheaper and the solar_duck_curve strategy prioritizes charging during the mid-day solar-cheap period rather than discharging. With Battery SOC at 90% (0.9) and general rules enforcing a 95% charge ceiling, we avoid further discharge (so shave_kw=0) and instead target bringing SOC up toward 95% to prepare for the upcoming late-afternoon/evening surge while keeping at least 25% SOC reserve for safety/lifecycle. This also prevents unnecessary cycle wear by not discharging during the cheapest energy procurement window.

optimization_strategy.strategy_name: Solar Duck Curve (Phase 2: Duck Ramp) — PEAK tariff discharge
optimization_strategy.rationale: Tariff_window is PEAK and day_type is solar_duck_curve at 14:00. The solar-duck-curve strategy prioritizes preventing early discharge that would waste later duck-ramp value, but at 14:00 the forecasted load is already far above MD (forecast ≈ 899–916 kW vs MD limit 800 kW). To avoid any MD breach during a high-cost PEAK window, we discharge at the max allowed per interval (100 kW) to bring net load toward/under the MD limit while respecting SOC safety. With SOC at 90% (0.90) and a required reserve of 25% SOC (soft minimum for duck-ramp), discharging 100 kW for one interval is consistent with keeping reserve at 25% and avoids SOC going below 10%. Forecast confidence is high (0.95), so aggressive shaving is justified to protect the demand-charge (MD) risk.

optimization_strategy.strategy_name: Solar Duck Curve (Phase 2: Duck Ramp smoothing, 15:00-19:00) — applied conservatively at 14:30
optimization_strategy.rationale: Tariff window is PEAK (RM 0.45/kWh), but day_type is solar_duck_curve and current time is 14:30 (within the solar valley window). The Solar Duck Curve strategy specifies no discharge during the valley period (10:00-15:00) and emphasizes preserving SOC until the 15:00 ramp. Current load forecast values are ~906–922 kW, and MD limit is 800 kW, so shaving would be beneficial economically; however, discharging before 15:00 would waste the duck-curve timing advantage and conflicts with the strategy constraint. With SOC at 85.25% (above the required reserve), the optimal action at 14:30 is to hold (shave_kw=0) and position capacity for the 15:00-19:00 period where aggressive discharge (30-60 kW class) is permitted. Cycle count is very low (0.025), so degradation limits are not constraining. Confidence is limited slightly because the aggressive peak-shaving strategy could reduce MD risk earlier, but duck-curve timing rules are higher priority for this day_type.
constraints: max_100kW_interval (from peak strategy; not used due to 0 shave)

optimization_strategy.strategy_name: Solar Duck Curve - Aggressive evening duck-ramp discharge with PEAK shaving
optimization_strategy.rationale: Tariff window is PEAK and day_type is solar_duck_curve at 15:00, which matches the duck-ramp phase (15:00-19:00) for aggressive discharge to blunt the late-afternoon surge. Forecast load at this tick is ~871.97–892.94 kW, while MD limit is 800 kW, so peak shaving is required to avoid MD breach risk. With battery SOC at 85.25% (>35% and well above 20% soft minimum), we can discharge while maintaining reserve SOC. Using the solar_duck_curve rule to discharge 30–60 kW, combined with general aggressive peak-shaving needs to mitigate MD overrun, we cap discharge at the allowed max interval rate (100 kW). This reduces the effective load by ~100 kW (bringing it toward/closer to the MD limit) while keeping SOC above the 20% reserve and remaining in a safe degradation regime given the very low cycle count.

Tariff window is PEAK with a solar_duck_curve day type at 15:30, which falls into the duck-ramp period (15:00–19:00) where late-afternoon surge smoothing is prioritized. Load forecast is [881.23, 900.19, 896.89] kW, with MD limit 800.0 kW, so there is a direct PEAK demand-charge risk. To keep the next interval(s) from exceeding MD, target shaving of (forecast_peak - MD) plus a small buffer is required. Using the first forecast point: shave_kw = 881.23 - 800.0 - 0.0 ≈ 81.23 kW. SOC is high at 81.8% (>=35% trigger), and cycle count is very low (0.043), so lifecycle constraints are not restrictive (0–2000 cycles normal operation). Safety: maintain at least 20% hard minimum and use the duck-curve reserve target of 25% SOC; the chosen target_soc_end (50%) provides ample headroom to avoid getting trapped before the end of the ramp while still achieving MD compliance. Confidence reduced slightly because the provided PEAK strategy files assume a weekday model, while the day_type here is solar_duck_curve (timing matters), but forecast confidence is high (0.95).

optimization_strategy.strategy_name: Solar Duck Curve (PEAK ramp) - Aggressive evening discharge
optimization_strategy.rationale: Tariff window is PEAK (RM 0.45/kWh on weekdays 08:00–22:00). At 16:00 the forecasted load is ~880 kW (solar_duck_curve) and exceeds the MD limit (800 kW), so we must aggressively shave during the late-afternoon ramp to avoid or reduce any MD breach. Battery SOC is high at 78% (>35% and >40%), and cycle count (~0.063) is in normal range (0–2000 cycles), so full discharge depth is allowed by lifecycle rules. The solar_duck_curve strategy prioritizes blunting the evening surge starting after 15:00; therefore we discharge at the max interval limit of 100 kW while keeping SOC above the soft minimum reserve. This discharge brings the projected SOC from 78% to ~58% (>=20% reserve), reducing the interval load from ~880 kW to ~780 kW, bringing it below MD.
constraints: respect_cycle_budget (cycle count well within 0–2000 normal operation)

optimization_strategy.strategy_name: Solar Duck Curve (Phase 2 Duck Ramp smoothing during PEAK)
optimization_strategy.rationale: Tariff is PEAK (RM 0.45/kWh, 08:00–22:00) and day_type is solar_duck_curve. At 16:30, this is within the duck-ramp window (after 15:00) where the strategy calls for aggressive discharge to blunt the late-afternoon surge. Forecast load is 873.65 kW with MD limit 800.0 kW, so to avoid a demand-charge breach we need to shave at least 873.65-800.0 = 73.65 kW. SOC is 74.1% (>35% rule / >20% reserve requirement), and cycle count is low (~0.083), so normal (not degraded) operation is allowed. We therefore set shave_kw to exactly cover the MD margin while maintaining SOC reserve (25% minimum) and targeting end-of-interval SOC ~70% to avoid overuse risk and keep headroom for continuing PEAK shaving in subsequent intervals.
